newsitem.title: UK: Oil city Aberdeen set to explore beyond North Sea.
newsitem.headline: Oil city Aberdeen set to explore beyond North Sea.

text.p: The North Sea oil rush of the 1960s catapulted Aberdeen on Scotland's northeast coast from a sleepy seaside city to a boom town fuelled by petrodollars.
Now, as Britain's offshore sector reaches its twilight years, the city is trying to reinvent itself as a hi-tech support centre to serve the cost-conscious international oil industry of the future.
Employment in both the offshore and onshore oil sectors has been on the decline since the mid-1980s, when a slide in oil prices spawned a wave of cost saving measures.

"In 1986 the oil price fell and you found that in the high cost time you built in a lot of redundancy that in time you realised you really didn't need," George Watkins, chairman and managing director of Aberdeen-based Conoco UK Ltd, told Reuters.

Cost-cutting initiatives like the Cost Reduction Initiative for the New Era (CRINE), launched four years ago, brought offshore operating costs in the North Sea down to 2.64 stg per barrel in 1996, their lowest levels for 10 years, said consultants Wood Mackenzie.

Coupled with new technologies, such measures have increased the life expectancy of the North Sea oil industry by years, and should to take production in the UK sector to record levels of nearly 2.8 million barrels per day in 1997.
But after this year oil output is set to fall again, pulling employment levels down further.

Aberdeenshire Council forecasts that the offshore workforce in the northern and central North Sea will fall from 20,500 in 1996 to 18,000 in 2006, while oil industry jobs in northeast Scotland -- mainly concentrated in Aberdeen -- will drop by 1,500 to 22,000.

"It is generally predicted that there will be a decline in employment. Things are changing, the skills required for tomorrow's industry will be different," said Louise MacDonald of the Aberdeen-based Scottish Enterprise Energy Group.
With this in mind, Aberdeen is seeking to establish itself as a research and development centre for the oil industry world-wide.

"We want to anchor that skill set here and effectively have a nucleus of companies that can operate all over the world...Manufacturing will become transplantable, but the knowledge-based side is something that will last," MacDonald said.
Heading up these efforts is Aberdeen's offshore technology park where research is underway into techniques for pumping oil in deep waters such as the West of Shetlands area in the British Atlantic.
The research aims to devise new anchoring systems and ways of connecting pipelines to carry oil from the sea bed to floating production vessels used in place of fixed installations.

"Technology for deepwater drilling West of Shetland was developed in Aberdeen, which couldn't be done four of five years ago," Iain Bell, chief executive of the Offshore Contractors Association (OCA) told Reuters.
But progress so far on the export front has been slow.

Last month Martin Stanley, head of the government's Oil, Gas and Petroleum Supplies Office (OSO), told delegates at a CRINE network conference in Aberdeen that British exports accounted for just one percent of the 60 billion stg spent per year on goods and services by the international oil industry outside the U.K.

"The statistics show exports to be poor, but I believe this has been recognised and things are moving forward," said Dan Stover, the head of U.S. energy major Brown & Root's production services in Aberdeen. "There is a lot of energy in the service sector (in Aberdeen) towards leveraging itself into the international market from here."

The key to success will be continued focus on costs, local industry sources said. "Aberdeen can do it, but it has to get its price right. It has to make sure it doesn't price itself out of the market," said the OCA's Bell.
